headline: High: shared filesystem and overlapping write/MCP/browser-capable coding agents create prompt-injection, data-leakage, and action-conflict risks by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Devin can use MCP, read/write files, and shares state via integrations; Windsurf can read/write workspace files, use MCP, and shares state via the local filesystem. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if one agent consumes the other's files or outputs. The pathway is not proven to be fully automatic, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF either agent reads the other agent's generated files as instructions
IF a shared workspace or synced folder is mounted between the two agents
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Disable automatic file ingestion between agents
Use a human review step before copying outputs
Restrict MCP servers to read-only where possible

B_data_leakage.rationale: Devin touches source code, issue trackers, team chat, and docs, while Windsurf touches source code and open files. Both have broad network egress and file access, so sensitive material in shared code or workspace files can flow into either agent's context and then out through their respective backends. The shared-file path is explicit for Windsurf and integration sharing is explicit for Devin.
conditions: IF both agents can access the same repository checkout or workspace files
IF sensitive data is present in files either agent opens or edits
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared workspaces
Use separate repos or clones per agent
Redact sensitive files before agent access
Limit network egress during sensitive tasks

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands, modify git state, write filesystems, and use MCP. Devin's shared_state_with_other_instances is via integrations, while Windsurf shares state via the local filesystem. Concurrent writes to the same repo or workspace can corrupt git state or overwrite each other's changes, and no locking mechanism is documented here. This matches the high-risk overlap pattern.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git checkout or workspace directory
IF neither orchestrator enforces file or git locks
mitigations: Assign one agent per branch
Pause one agent before the other writes
Use git worktrees or separate clones
Enable explicit locking around shared files
Review and merge changes manually

D_cascading_error.rationale: Devin is a long-running planner-executor and Windsurf is a Cascade agentic IDE with auto-execute opt-in, so one agent's output can become the other's input and then trigger actions. However, Windsurf defaults to approval per command, which reduces but does not eliminate cascading mistakes. The interaction is plausible in default workflows, but not clearly fully autonomous.
conditions: IF Devin's generated plan or code is pasted into Windsurf without verification
IF Windsurf auto-execute is enabled or command approvals are bypassed
mitigations: Require human verification of handoffs
Disable auto-execute
Add a checklist for code and command review
Use tests before applying generated changes

E_compliance.rationale: Devin explicitly handles team chat, issue trackers, docs, and integration tokens, while Windsurf handles source code and open files with model-provider keys optional. The profiles do not specify a residency or certification mismatch, so only a limited compliance concern is visible: mixed data classes and secrets in a closed-source pair. I do not cite only one agent because the risk is about the pair's combined handling.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared code or workspace files
IF either agent is used on data subject to stricter retention or residency rules
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared workspaces
Document data-class boundaries
Rotate any exposed tokens
Use separate retention policies per workspace
